Saddle-shaped hollow in the skull base that holds the pituitary (sella turcica).
Organ that makes and releases substances such as hormones.
The visible outer ear flap.
Notch where vessels and nerves enter an organ such as the lung or kidney.
The nostrils.

Chalky urate deposits under the skin in chronic gout.
Round bacteria, plural. Staph and strep are the famous ones. Yes, three Cs. No, that’s not a typo.
Unit of magnetic field strength. Most MRI scanners run at 1.5 or 3 of them.
Newborn score out of 10, checked at 1 and 5 minutes after birth.

Ankle bone that links the leg to the foot.
Bundle of fibres carrying signals between the brain and body.
Shin bone. The larger of the two lower-leg bones.

Hard structure in the jaw for biting and chewing.
C-shaped cartilage cushion in the knee, two per knee. Tears with a twist on a planted foot, a classic footy and netball injury.
Sudden confusion with wandering attention that comes and goes, often triggered by infection, medicines or surgery in older people. A medical emergency, not ‘just old age’.
Pain shooting from the buttock down the back of the leg, from an irritated sciatic nerve (often a bulging lumbar disc). Most cases settle on their own within weeks to a few months.
Old unit of radioactivity, named after Marie and Pierre Curie.
Optic nerve damage, often with raised eye pressure, that quietly steals side vision first. Usually painless, so regular eye checks matter.
